title: A minimally invasive technique for serial intraosseous perfusion measurements in the murine tibia using laser Doppler flowmetry
author: Hanne, Easter, et al.
materials: 1.Connect the LDF monitor to a computer. Turn on the LDF monitor and open the data acquisition software provided by the manufacturer. In the signal processing settings, reduce the bandwidth to one appropriate for the slower blood speeds in rodent bone, about 0.4–1 mm/s [3], by selecting a lower cutoff frequency for the low-pass filter (e.g., 3 kHz) [8], as suggested by the manufacturer. Note: Perfusion data captured with different bandwidth settings should not be compared.2.Clean the LDF probe with 70% ethanol using a sterile cotton swab and allow to air dry.

steps.title: Fast mice before procedure
steps.instruction: Fast each 14‑week‑old male C57Bl/6J mouse for 6–8 h prior to the experiment.

steps.title: Calibrate and clean LDF monitor
steps.instruction: Connect the LDF monitor to a computer, turn it on, open the manufacturer’s acquisition software, and set the low‑pass filter cutoff to ~3 kHz to achieve a bandwidth of 0.4–1 mm/s. Do not compare data recorded with different bandwidths. Calibrate the monitor with a probe‑flux standard according to the manufacturer’s directions; calibrate between studies, not between individual LDF recordings. Clean the LDF probe with a sterile cotton swab soaked in 70 % ethanol and let it air‑dry.

substeps.instruction: Connect monitor, power on, launch software.
Set low‑pass filter cutoff to ~3 kHz (bandwidth 0.4–1 mm/s).
Calibrate with probe‑flux standard (between studies only).
Wipe probe with 70 % ethanol, air‑dry.

steps.title: Induce anesthesia and position mouse
steps.instruction: Place the mouse in an induction chamber and anesthetize with isoflurane 3–5 % in pure oxygen (alternatives such as compressed air may alter perfusion and should not be compared). Shave the fur over the anterior and medial surfaces of the proximal tibia and knee joint. Position the mouse supine on a heated surgical pad, tape the hind paws to expose the medial hindlimb, maintain anesthesia at 1.5–2 % isoflurane, keep rectal temperature at 37 °C with a feedback‑controlled heater, and apply ophthalmic ointment to the eyes.

substeps.instruction: Induce with isoflurane 3–5 % in O₂.
Shave fur over proximal tibia and knee.
Place mouse supine on heated pad, tape hind paws.
Maintain isoflurane 1.5–2 %, rectal temp 37 °C.
Apply ophthalmic ointment.

steps.title: Disinfect surgical site
steps.instruction: Disinfect the planned incision area three times with povidone‑iodine followed by 70 % ethanol.

steps.title: Identify incision location
steps.instruction: Palpate the anterior surface of the proximal tibia with forceps to locate the most proximal anteromedial bone surface that lies directly under the skin without intervening soft tissue; re‑tape the limb if needed to keep this site accessible.

steps.title: Make skin incision
steps.instruction: Using a #11 (or similar) scalpel blade, create a 2–5 mm sagittal incision over the proximal tibia, starting ~3–4 mm distal to the knee and moving distally. Absorb any fluid with a sterile cotton‑tipped applicator. If bleeding occurs, hold a sterile cotton applicator or gauze on the site for 15–30 s until it stops.

substeps.instruction: Make 2–5 mm incision 3–4 mm below knee.
Absorb fluid with sterile cotton tip.
Control bleeding by applying pressure 15–30 s if needed.

steps.title: Expose bone and remove periosteum
steps.instruction: Gently retract any soft tissue covering the tibia with forceps. Using the edge of the scalpel blade, scrape a small periosteal window roughly the size of the LDF probe tip (≈0.8 mm diameter). Probe the surface with the scalpel to confirm periosteum removal; the bone will feel stiffer after removal.

substeps.instruction: Retract soft tissue with forceps.
Scrape periosteum to create ~0.8 mm window.
Confirm removal by probing the bone surface.

steps.title: Position LDF probe
steps.instruction: Mount the micromanipulator and place the LDF probe tip into the periosteum‑free window, pressing gently so the tip is firmly against and perpendicular to the exposed bone surface. Apply only enough force to prevent probe slipping; avoid excessive pressure that could lower perfusion readings. Do not touch the probe or fiber‑optic cable while recording.

steps.title: Record perfusion reading
steps.instruction: Capture a 30‑second perfusion trace with the LDF software. Interpret the reading: <5 perfusion units (PU) indicates improper perpendicular placement; >30 PU suggests the probe has slipped into soft tissue; signal variation >5 PU indicates motion or poor contact. If any of these occur, reposition the probe and repeat until a stable signal is obtained.

substeps.instruction: Record 30 s perfusion trace.
Check PU value: <5 PU → reposition; >30 PU → reposition; variation >5 PU → reposition.
Re‑position as needed for a stable signal.

steps.title: Repeat probe placement for averaging
steps.instruction: Remove the probe, reposition it in the same window, and record a second 30‑second reading. If the two readings differ by more than 5 PU, acquire additional readings and calculate the average perfusion for the session.

substeps.instruction: Remove and reposition probe.
Record second 30 s reading.
If difference >5 PU, take extra readings and average.

steps.title: Close incision with adhesive
steps.instruction: After the final reading, pinch the incision closed with forceps, apply a small amount of tissue adhesive to the exterior of the wound, and hold the tissue together for 15 s. Avoid contacting the adhesive with the forceps or placing it inside the incision.

substeps.instruction: Pinch incision with forceps.
Apply minimal tissue adhesive to outside only.
Hold for 15 s.

steps.title: Apply postoperative topical agents
steps.instruction: Apply a thin layer of 2 % lidocaine cream followed by triple‑antibiotic ointment to the closed incision site.

steps.title: Recover mouse and monitor
steps.instruction: Remove the hind‑limb tape and the rectal temperature probe, turn off the isoflurane, and place the mouse in a heated recovery cage until it is ambulatory. Return the animal to its home cage and check for signs of discomfort twice daily for at least 48 hours (longer if needed).

substeps.instruction: Remove tape and rectal probe.
Turn off isoflurane.
Transfer to heated recovery cage until ambulatory.
Return to home cage; monitor twice daily for ≥48 h.

description: Our modified LDF technique is based on a procedure that has been proven to measure perfusion accurately in the murine tibia, demonstrated by comparing LDF readings to controlled blood flow rates through ex vivo bone samples using a syringe pump [3]. Greater cortical thickness will have a lower LDF perfusion measurement, but small variations in cortical thickness do not greatly affect perfusion readings [3]. Therefore, LDF readings should only be compared when cortical thickness is not expected to be significantly different, whether with age, sex, mouse strain, treatment, or other conditions. The modified method described above does not yield quantitative blood flow measurements, but if cortical thickness were measured with microcomputed tomography, then blood flow rate could be estimated using the empirically derived equation in the original study [3]. We have shown that this modified technique can be used serially in the same mice without inducing inflammation or gait abnormalities [7]. We performed the modified technique in two groups of male C57Bl/6J mice starting at 12 weeks of age. One group received weekly tibial perfusion measurements for four weeks (n = 10, Repeated), while the other group only had tibial perfusion measured at the fourth week (n = 8, Endpoint). We found no difference in tibial perfusion between the Repeated and Endpoint groups at the end of the study (t-test p = 0.92, Fig. 3), demonstrating that repeated LDF procedures do not affect subsequent measurements, at least up to four weeks.
